claim: **A production ML system is mostly not the model.** The authors state that a model usually contains only about five per cent of the code required to put an ML application into production.

**Production ML differs from research ML on data, priorities and lifetime.** Research ML uses a static dataset, one design priority and a single terminal result; production ML uses shifting real-world data, several competing priorities, and continuous monitoring, assessment and retraining.

**Training data must cover the feature space of the prediction requests the system will actually receive**, and coverage density matters as much as example count because duplicated or near-duplicated examples add no information.
**Encoding ambiguity is a data defect with the same status as a missing value.** The authors' example is an elevation reading of zero that may mean sea level or may mean that no measurement arrived.
**Where one model's output is another model's input, errors propagate over time**, which makes upstream model monitoring a dependency of downstream model correctness.

**Drift and skew are different comparisons and should not be conflated.** Drift compares successive iterations of one data source over time; skew compares two different sources, characteristically training against serving.

**Data drift is a change in the distribution of the input features; concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and labels.** Concept drift invalidates the mapping the model learned rather than merely moving the inputs.
**Skew decomposes into schema skew, feature skew and distribution skew**, which are detected by different mechanisms and have different remedies.

**The rate at which ground truth changes determines the labelling strategy.** Change over months or years permits crowd-based curated datasets; change over days or hours forces direct feedback or weak supervision.

**Training–serving skew is caused by performing different preprocessing at training and at serving**, and the authors describe it as a common production failure that is hard to detect because the model continues to return plausible answers.

**The structural remedy for training–serving skew is to export the preprocessing as a graph and attach it to the served model**, so that full-pass statistics computed once at training are applied element-wise at serving by the same code.

**Transformations divide into instance-level and full-pass**, and only the former can be computed from a single serving request, so full-pass results must be stored as constants and shipped with the model.

**Aggregate metrics conceal subgroup failure, and which slices matter is a domain-knowledge question rather than a statistical one.** Slicing on metadata the model does not consume can be more informative than slicing on model features.

**ML systems are sensitive in two ways ordinary software tests do not catch: entanglement, where changing one feature changes the whole model, and configuration, where a small error in hyperparameters, versions or feature lists silently changes behaviour.**

**Observability in ML is imported from control theory, where a system can only be controlled to the extent that it can be observed**, and is operationalised through alertability, meaning metrics and thresholds that make failure unambiguous, and actionability, meaning enough signal to support root cause analysis.

**Monitoring splits into functional monitoring of predictive performance and serving-data distributions, and non-functional monitoring of latency, failures and resource use**, and the second matters independently of the first because a system that is down serves no predictions at all.

**Drift detection splits into supervised techniques that require fresh labels and unsupervised techniques that do not**, the latter being the practical default because labelling is slow and expensive.

**Retraining policy is a design decision with no correct answer.** The authors report that scheduled retraining is common because it is simple and often adequate, while noting that it assumes a steady rate of change in the world which frequently does not hold.
**Latency, throughput and cost trade against each other and against accuracy**, and the authors state as a general rule that shorter latency costs more.

**For online serving, latency rather than accuracy is usually the binding requirement**, so a simpler model that clears the accuracy bar is preferred to a more accurate model that does not clear the latency bar.

**Model complexity should be added against a fixed serving infrastructure and a declared gating metric**, so that complexity stops when an operational constraint such as latency or model size is breached rather than when improvement stops.

**Optimisation techniques trade accuracy for resource cost, and the size of the loss is specific to the model and data and hard to predict in advance.** Quantisation, pruning and knowledge distillation each reduce size or latency at some accuracy cost that must be measured rather than assumed.

**Neural networks do learn to suppress uninformative features, but the suppressed capacity is still stored, still traversed at inference and still requires the feature to be collected and maintained for the life of the product.**

**MLOps extends DevOps in two specific ways: continuous integration must validate data, schemas and models rather than only code, and continuous delivery ships a pipeline that produces a prediction service rather than shipping a model.**
**The authors describe MLOps maturity as levels 0, 1 and 2 defined by how much of the workflow is automated**, and mark level 2 as still somewhat speculative at the time of writing.
**There is no industry-standard scheme for versioning models.** The authors propose a major, minor and pipeline scheme and describe several incompatible alternatives in current use.

**Lineage is what makes a model reproducible, comparable across runs, and deletable on request.** Recording artefacts, executions and contexts turns provenance questions into queries rather than investigations.

**Live experimentation exists because model metrics are not business metrics.** A recommender trained to maximise click-through is optimising a labelled proxy for a profit objective that was never in the training data.
**Equal fairness metrics across groups do not establish that a system is fair**, and fairness evaluation must be repeated through development and after launch rather than treated as a release gate.

**Interpretability has no mathematical definition and is not cleanly separable from explainability**, so the working definition the authors adopt requires only that a human can understand the model's operations through introspection or a produced explanation.
**Privacy costs accuracy, computation time, or both**, and the cheapest control is not collecting the data in the first place.
**A deletion request may force a retrain**, which makes data and model lineage a precondition for satisfying data-protection obligations rather than an optional engineering nicety.
**Pipeline orchestration is required because components have ordering dependencies and because expensive completed steps must be cached so that a failure reruns only the failing component.**
**Not every project needs a pipeline.** Pipelines are unnecessary for pure experimentation and become necessary once a model has users and therefore requires continuous update.

**The book's closing position is to reason about ML systems rather than ML models**, the diagnostic questions being how users interact with the model, whether they can report misclassifications, and whether that feedback reaches retraining.
Observe activity where it occurs; do not substitute requested features or generalized self-report for design data.
Interpret with the person and then again with the cross-functional team.
Consolidate inductively before claiming population patterns.
Use multiple models because each representation reveals and hides different structure.
Keep ideas visibly connected to evidence through the Wall Walk.
Generate several visions before converging on product concepts.
Alternate scenario thinking and structural thinking throughout detailed design.
Define places and purposes before widgets; define interface architecture before visual detail.
Treat every design as a hypothesis and prototypes as instruments for discovering where it fails.
Resolve validation findings from practice to product structure to interaction structure to interface detail.
Slice releases by coherent user value, then prioritize function within the slice.
Keep the user-facing architecture available to implementation teams so local decisions preserve the whole.
The thesis is two sentences: focus on the domain and domain logic; base complex domain designs on a model.
Two practices are **prerequisites**, not recommendations: iterative development, and a continuing close relationship between developers and domain experts.
Knowledge crunching is joint modelling under correction, led by developers; it is not requirements elicitation.
The engineer's goal is not to become a domain expert but to "talk to experts, understand the major concepts relevant to the application, and sanity-check what we were building."
The ubiquitous language exists to eliminate translation, because translation creates bilingual bottlenecks whose "translations are inexact."
The language is the customer's jargon **cleaned up** — sharper and narrower — with the experts holding a veto if the cleaning distorts accepted field meaning.
A change to the language is a change to the model, and must ripple into the code.
Speaking scenarios aloud is a first-class modelling technique; "Rough edges are easy to hear."
Sophisticated domain experts must understand the core of the model; technical components are explicitly exempt.
Multiple dialects are expected; the division that must never exist is between experts and developers.
Model-driven design requires a modelling paradigm with tool support and has "limited applicability" in purely procedural languages.
Anyone contributing to the model must touch the code; specialised roles remain legitimate.
Aggregates are consistency boundaries with a single root controlling all access, making it practical to enforce invariants on every state change.
Deep models arrive through many small refactorings punctuated by occasional breakthroughs; a breakthrough "is not a technique; it is an event."
Never adopt a model a domain expert would not use, however elegant it seems.
Total model unification across a large enterprise "will not be feasible or cost-effective."
A bounded context is bounded in team organisation, application usage and physical artefacts — not merely in namespaces; a module is not a context.
Duplicate concepts and false cognates are the two failure signatures inside a context.
Context maps describe reality first; "don't change the map until the change in reality is done."
Context boundaries follow team and political contours as much as technical ones.
Conformity to a good upstream model is chosen "less often than we probably should" and can drag you into a better design.
An anticorruption layer translates concepts, not messages, and its isolation must be costed.
Non-integration is a legitimate, often correct, answer.
The core domain is relative to point of view, cannot usually be purchased, should be made small, and should get the best people.
Generic subdomains should not be designed for reuse.
Large-scale structure must evolve; imposing it up front is likely to be costly.
Strategic design requires minimalism and humility, and architecture teams must not absorb all the strongest people.
**Change the game:** reject the false choice between hard positional pressure and soft concession.
**Two-level diagnosis:** keep substantive issues distinct from relationship and process issues; negotiate both on their merits.
**Perception before persuasion:** reconstruct the choice and consequences as the other side sees them.
**Interests behind positions:** ask why and why not; list multiple material, relational, identity, and constituent interests.
**Concrete flexibility:** state interests precisely while treating any particular solution as revisable.
**Invent before deciding:** use explicit no-commitment option generation, then improve and evaluate candidates later.
**Dovetail differences:** trade across forecasts, valuations, timing, risk, scope, and priorities rather than split one number.
**Make their decision easy:** design an agreement the counterpart can implement and explain to constituents.
**Objective criteria and fair procedures:** reason from standards independent of either side's will; examine competing standards rather than invoking “fairness” as a slogan.
**BATNA:** develop and select the best action available without agreement; compare packages against it.
**Trip wire:** predefine a threshold that forces reassessment before a poor agreement is accepted.
**Micro-BATNA:** prepare what to do if this meeting ends without agreement.
**Negotiation jujitsu:** redirect positions, criticism, and personal attack into questions about interests, options, and standards.
**Questions and silence:** use inquiry to surface reasoning, then leave room for an answer.
**One-text procedure:** iterate one draft through criticism when competing proposals cause positional lock-in.
**Negotiate the process:** name suspected tactics, test them, and agree rules before proceeding.
**Framework agreement:** expose unresolved terms early and draft toward operational commitments.
**Seven sources of power:** relationship, communication/process, interests, options, legitimacy, BATNA, and commitment.
**Question quality is owned by the interviewer.** Socially generous respondents are a predictable condition, not an excuse for weak evidence.
**Facts before opinions.** Recent episodes, actual workflows, current costs, prior attempts, and allocated resources are more useful than approval or prediction.
**Importance before detail.** Establish that the problem category is active and consequential before ranking needs inside it.
**Problem ownership and solution ownership differ.** Stakeholders supply evidence about their lives; the product team remains responsible for design judgement.
**Deflect, anchor, dig.** Redirect compliments, ground generic and future claims in past specifics, and investigate the cause beneath requests and emotions.
**Expose the dangerous assumption.** Ask what would cause failure and what must be true for success; include legal, budget, adoption, distribution, and technical dependencies.
**Choose the evidence mechanism by risk.** Conversation can investigate market and customer uncertainty; product risk requires prototypes, technical spikes, usage, or other direct tests.
**Commitment is costly behaviour.** Interpret time, reputation, and money relative to what the particular stakeholder is actually sacrificing.
**Advancement needs a named next state.** A warm meeting without a decision, owner, condition, or next action is not pipeline progress.
**Segmentation makes evidence comparable.** Mixed answers across unlike populations should not be aggregated as one customer voice.
**A useful segment is findable.** Pair a specific kind of person or organisation with the place or behaviour through which they can be reached.
**Learning is a team state.** Shared preparation, first-hand exposure, retrievable notes, and immediate review prevent one person becoming the repository of customer truth.
**Speed means resolving the next uncertainty.** The three-question list changes as beliefs change; conversations stop when they cease adding relevant information.
Change happens one person at a time; "Successful change, at its core, is rooted in something much simpler: How to facilitate change with one person."
The five elements are building blocks: "All five elements must be in place for a change to be realized", and they "must occur in sequence and they are cumulative."
The ordering argument is **entailment, not evidence** — desire cannot precede awareness, knowledge cannot precede desire, and so on down the chain.
The model "begins after a change has been identified" and says nothing about whether the change is right.
Awareness covers the nature of the change, the reason for it, the risk of not changing, the internal and external drivers, **and** "what's in it for me" — it is not only the *why*.
Communicating is not the same as producing awareness: "Awareness is not achieved based on the messages sent, but rather how the messages are received and internalized by each person."
Reception is governed by five factors, of which contestability of the stated reasons is the one teams most often ignore.
Desire is "ultimately about personal choice" and "by definition, not under our direct control"; assuming it follows from awareness is the named executive error.
The correct first move against resistance is to identify the barrier point, then "stop talking and start listening".
Knowledge is not the starting point; training aimed past an awareness or desire barrier does not work.
Knowledge is not ability: ability is "turning knowledge into action" at "the required performance levels", and some people never reach it.
Ability requires practice, time, coaching, obstacle removal and "a safe environment to practice new skills and job roles".
An unopened feedback channel makes a broken system look like a failing employee.
Reinforcement must be meaningful, tied to real accomplishment, free of countervailing consequences, and backed by accountability in day-to-day operations.
The barrier point is "the first element of the model that is weak or would be assessed as 'low'" — operationally, the first element scoring 3 or below on an anonymous 1–5 self-rating.

Hiatt's own statements about effort past the barrier are conditional ("will not by itself", "will not be productive until"), with one absolute exception: "In the absence of desire, no amount of knowledge can produce change."
The model is offered as a lens over existing practice, not as a replacement for it, and explicitly not as a prescribed process.
The elements apply to customers, suppliers, the public and school communities, not only to employees.
The eight errors are the diagnosis and the eight stages are their inversion; Kotter presents the diagnosis first, and it is the more transferable half.

The order matters "usually", and concurrency is expected: all efforts end up "operating in multiple stages at once", and a large transformation contains smaller projects each running the whole sequence.
Complacency is the default condition and is systemic rather than a defect of individuals; nine specific sources are named, most of them measurement and feedback failures.

Urgency may legitimately be manufactured. Engineered crises, deliberately accepted unrealistic targets and permitted failures are all endorsed, with a stated preference for opportunity-based routes where they will work.
A guiding coalition is selected for position power, expertise, credibility and leadership; a coalition of managers only is said to guarantee failure; large egos and "snakes" are excluded outright.
A usable vision is "explained within five minutes" and gets a reaction showing "both understanding and interest".
The vision is undercommunicated by orders of magnitude, and inconsistent behaviour by senior people "overwhelms other forms of communication".
Visible inconsistencies that cannot be removed must be explained aloud rather than defended.
Empowerment is barrier removal across four named categories — structures, skills, systems, supervisors — with HR systems singled out.
Short-term wins are planned, not hoped for; they must be visible, unambiguous and clearly attributable, and they are also a test of the vision.
Wins are dangerous. Celebration is the mechanism by which resisters end change efforts.
Interdependence is why the process needs eight stages: "you have to change nearly everything".
Culture changes at the end, only after new behaviour has visibly produced better results and the link has been made explicit; succession and promotion decide whether it holds.
Management produces consistency and leadership produces change, and transformation is over-managed and under-led; but stage 6 in particular fails without competent management.
**Interviewing is skilled, asymmetric inquiry.** A conversational tone coexists with deliberate control of purpose, pacing, follow-up, and attention.
**Check the team's worldview at the door.** Externalize assumptions before fieldwork so they can be noticed without making confirmation the session's job.
**Study behavior and meaning together.** A sequence without rationale is incomplete; a stated rationale without observed context may be idealized.
**Reframe without abandoning the brief.** A deeper problem can extend the commissioned question, but the team remains accountable for the original decision need.
**Use the participant's context and language.** Artifacts, interruptions, social relations, terminology, and misperceptions are part of the evidence.
**Prepare to improvise.** Objectives, screening, a field guide, roles, logistics, consent, and equipment make responsible flexibility possible.
**Treat recruiting as research data.** Scarcity, ambiguity, and mismatched contexts can falsify assumptions about the population or workflow.
**Ask, show, enact, and make.** Demonstration, mapping, role-play, concepts, sorting, and homework expose different layers of a practice.
**Build rapport through attention.** Follow-ups, silence, body language, selective self-disclosure, and respect for social norms show that the participant matters.
**Silence is interpreted, not applied.** It can invite continuation, make room for thought, or signal confusion and distress depending on person and culture.
**Assume contradictions are intelligible.** Explore the missing distinction instead of accusing the participant or averaging the conflict away.
**Separate record from interpretation.** Notes, recordings, photographs, sketches, transcripts, highlights, and debriefs have different evidential roles.
**Analyze cases before extracting themes.** Preserve enough context to understand a participant, then synthesize across cases rather than collecting decontextualized quotes.
**Research impact is designed.** Stakeholder involvement, visible process, appropriate output forms, and an explicit chain from evidence to implication determine whether findings enter decisions.
**Agent 365 is a control plane over three pillars — observe, govern, secure — and five capabilities: registry, access control, visualisation, interoperability, security.**
**GA 1 May 2026**, commercial segment, **per user**, **USD 15 per user per month** standalone or included in **Microsoft 365 E7**. E5 named as the preferred prerequisite in the words "works best".
**A licence covers a human who manages, sponsors or is served by agents.** Cost scales with people, not with agent count.
**An agent identity is a single-tenant service principal with an "agent" subtype, and holds no credentials of its own.**
**The blueprint holds the credentials and impersonates the agent identity**; the agent identity holds the permissions and the audit identity.
**"A compromise of the blueprint's credentials affects all agent identities under it, which is why blueprint count is a security boundary decision."**
**A sponsor is required at creation for every agent identity and blueprint. Owners and managers are optional.**
**Sponsorship transfers automatically to the sponsor's manager on departure.**
**Sponsors act; they do not configure.** Enable, disable, soft-delete, change sponsors. No application settings. Owners re-enable, restore and hard-delete.
Limits: **100 sponsors** per agent identity or blueprint, **max 5 groups**; **5** per agent user account. Role-assignable and assigned-membership security groups are **not** permitted as sponsors.

**Interactive agents** use delegated permissions and the on-behalf-of flow; **autonomous agents** use client credentials. An **agent's user account** is optional, paired 1:1, and additive rather than substitutive.

**Service principals and regular user accounts are both explicitly not recommended**, with named failure modes for the latter: Conditional Access misapplied, ID Protection degraded, identity governance removing agent access.
**Agent activity logs under the base identity type.** Detection requires the **`agentType`** property; anything other than `notAgentic` means an agent was involved.
**Pre-platform agents still run on ordinary application service principals** and lack every agent-specific behaviour, including enforced sponsorship.
**Registry counts: total agents, agents without owners, unmanaged agents.** Ownerless is usually caused by staff departure, not misconduct.
**Ten named risk types**, of which three of the four Critical entries are governance failures rather than attacks.
**The Risks column shows only high-severity risks, and may lag the security portals by up to an hour.**
**The AI Administrator cannot investigate Defender or Purview risks. Nobody in the published role table can investigate Purview risks** without separate Insider Risk Management roles.
**Purview audit covers agent-to-agent and agent-to-tool. Purview DLP does not.**
**"Because an agent instance is unaware of the block action, the agent owner must actively monitor a DLP policy..."** — the agent is not told it was blocked.
**"Newly created content from Agent 365 doesn't inherit sensitivity labels from the source items."**
**Encryption without sensitivity labels is the single unsupported Purview capability.**
**DSPM for AI (classic) does not support Agent 365.** Use the current DSPM's **AI observability** page.
**Only audit, data classification and Compliance Manager AI assessments are automatic on agent creation.** Everything else must name the agent in a policy "as you would a user".
**Defender detection is in public preview.** Named threats: jailbreak, XPIA, malicious content propagation, secrets and credentials leak, evasion techniques, suspicious user access.
**Real-time protection rule detection types:** secret exfiltration, malicious content propagation, evasion techniques, unsafe email domain.
**"Agents that rely on unsupported tools or don't integrate with Work IQ MCP aren't covered."**
**Enabling blocking suppresses near-real-time alerts for that agent**; events become behaviours in `BehaviorInfo`.
**Six Advanced Hunting tables**; `AIAgentsInfo` deprecating in favour of `AgentsInfo`.
**Prompt evidence collection is on by default**, redacting secrets but not conversational sensitivity.
**Shadow AI detection is a list of seven named applications; only OpenClaw can be blocked**, only on Intune-managed Windows, with policy application taking **15 minutes to 8 hours**.
**Registry sync is preview, four platforms, manual trigger, long-lived third-party credentials including delete permissions.**
**Copilot Studio agents are governed automatically. Foundry agents sync automatically and may publish as autopilots. Everything else requires the Agent 365 SDK — a code change.**
**Data residency differs: Foundry follows the Azure region, Agent 365 follows the Entra tenant.** Data crosses models on ingestion.
**All 30-day metrics start at licence activation and are not backfilled.**
**Draft agents are visible only for Copilot Studio.**
**Three design principles:** provider-agnostic, zero friction, progressive disclosure.
**Three core types:** `EvalItem` (one conversation, split into query and response), `Evaluator` (scores items), `EvalResults` (aggregated pass/fail counts, per-item detail, portal links).
**Two evaluator tiers:** `LocalEvaluator` for inner-loop and CI smoke tests without API calls; `FoundryEvals` for cloud LLM-as-judge. **They can be mixed in one run.**
**`FoundryEvals` defaults to relevance, coherence and task adherence**, adding **tool call accuracy** automatically when tool definitions are present.

**Three split strategies:** **Last turn** (default; response quality at a point), **Full** (task completion and trajectory), **Per-turn** (fine-grained). Custom splitters accepted. **"How you split determines what you're evaluating."**
**Expected outputs** pair positionally with queries; **expected tool calls** can be specified separately.
**Pre-existing responses from logs can be evaluated without re-running the agent.**
**Repetitions** exist "to detect non-deterministic behavior".
**Workflow evaluation** extracts each sub-agent's interactions and evaluates them individually alongside the workflow's overall output.
**Agent behaviour evaluators:** `intent_resolution`, `task_adherence`, `task_completion`, `task_navigation_efficiency`.
**Tool usage evaluators:** `tool_call_accuracy`, `tool_selection`, `tool_input_accuracy`, `tool_output_utilization`, `tool_call_success`.
**Quality evaluators:** `coherence`, `fluency`, `relevance`, `groundedness`, `response_completeness`, `similarity`. **Safety evaluators:** `violence`, `sexual`, `self_harm`, `hate_unfairness`.
**`task_navigation_efficiency` takes `actions` and `expected_actions` and requires no model parameter** — the one deterministic agent-behaviour check.
**Customer Satisfaction uses six dimensions:** helpfulness, completeness, clarity, tone, resolution, adaptability.
**Output is pass/fail with a `reason`**, plus a numeric `score` for 1–5-scale evaluators; the documented example shows `tool_call_accuracy` 2 against threshold 3 failing.

**Data mapping:** `{{item.*}}` for dataset fields; `{{sample.output_items}}` for structured output including tool calls, required by the trajectory evaluators; `{{sample.output_text}}` for plain text.
Many evaluators are **preview**, and one consulted page is a superseded **classic** variant.
**The toolkit is a lifecycle harness.** Three stages — `provision`, `deploy`, `publish` — declared in `m365agents.yml`, with `m365agents.local.yml` and `m365agents.playground.yml` for other targets.
**The CLI is stated to offer the same features as the IDE extensions**, which is what makes automation credible.
**Scaffold shape:** `.vscode`, `appPackage`, `env`, `infra`, `src`. Two of the five hold generated infrastructure and identity configuration the developer will be asked to own.
**`atk upgrade` exists**, which is an admission that a generated project can fall out of step with its generator.
**`atk collaborator` and `atk uninstall` exist**, modelling shared ownership and estate cleanup as first-class commands.
**Environments are `.env.<target>` files with `${{VAR}}` substitution.** Secrets live in `.env.<target>.user`, never committed; CI injects `SECRET_*` at runtime.
**Target environment and agent version are the same mechanism.** A different Teams app ID makes two installable apps from one manifest, so v1 and v2 can run side by side in one tenant.
**Variant agent definitions are files in the repository reviewed in pull requests, not runtime feature flags.**
**Promotion is `--env`, not an edit.**
**The Playground removes the tenant, the tunnel and the registration** from the inner loop, and mocks Teams context, connector API responses and activities.
**Default channel differs by launch route:** `msteams` standalone, `emulator` through the toolkit — and `emulator` omits several Teams-specific activities.

**The Playground publishes its own limitations**, including no manifest processing, Adaptive Cards only with four features excluded, no mobile or meeting, and no typing indicator, tabs, message extensions, dialogs or single sign-on.
**The mock configuration requires exactly five users.** No rationale is published.
**`playground-cli` gives a headless `TestClient` and an HTTP conversation server** for CI. It drives conversations and asserts on them. **It does not evaluate.**
**Declarative agents have no local loop.** The Playground explicitly does not support them; `provision` into a licensed tenant is the inner loop.
**TypeSpec is an alternative authoring surface** for declarative agents and API plugins, compiling to manifests and OpenAPI, with eleven named capabilities.
**Omitting a capability's scoping array grants the whole surface the signed-in user can reach.** Narrowness is opt-in.
**The Agents SDK is transport, state and identity — not orchestration.** "The Agents SDK doesn't decide what an agent says."
**Languages:** C# on .NET 8.0; JavaScript on Node.js 18+; Python 3.9–3.11.

**Agent Framework composes inside the Agents SDK.** It merges Semantic Kernel and AutoGen orchestrators; the recommended pattern separates the orchestrating agent class from the `AgentApplication` managing `TurnContext`.
**"If you can write a function to handle the task, do that instead of using an AI agent."**
**Sample storage is in-memory and documented as needing replacement** with Blob or Cosmos DB for production.

**Bot Framework is superseded with detailed per-language migration guidance and a published unsupported list**, including Adaptive Dialogs, LUIS, QnA Maker, Composer, Language Generation, the Bot Framework CLI, streaming connections and QueueStorage.
**TeamsFx carries a dated window: community-only support until September 2026.**

**Distribution differs by build path on two axes.** Toolkit paths reach the commercial marketplace and cannot share person-to-person; Agent Builder, Copilot Studio declarative and SharePoint agents can share and cannot reach the marketplace.
**Publishing via the Agents Toolkit is unsupported in Microsoft 365 Government tenants.**

**Store gates are published and partly numeric** — manifest 1.13+, and 1.25+ for channel-operating agents from July 2026; stated latency percentiles; a stated availability figure; three to five sample prompts per command; mandatory AI label, citations and feedback button; `copilot` in `bot.scopes`; explicit user permission before API or MCP server calls.
**Store listing text is treated as an injection surface**, with instructional phrases, hidden characters and emojis prohibited in descriptions.
**Responsible AI manifest validation inspects the declared name, description and instructions** and blocks publication. It inspects nothing the agent does.
**The AI gateway "extends API Management's existing API gateway; it's not a separate offering."** Capability availability varies by service tier.

**Supported endpoint types:** OpenAI Chat Completions and Responses, Anthropic Messages (v2 tiers), Google Vertex AI; Foundry and non-Microsoft providers including Amazon Bedrock; remote MCP servers; A2A agent APIs; self-hosted models.
**Unified model API (preview):** multiple backends behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with automatic format translation and policy applied once.
**Five stated challenges:** authenticate and authorise; load balance; monitor and log; manage token usage and quotas across applications; enable developer self-service.

**Token limit policy:** TPM limits or quotas over hourly, daily, weekly, monthly or yearly periods; keyed on subscription key, originating IP, or an arbitrary policy expression; **prompt tokens can be precalculated at the gateway** to avoid backend calls that would exceed the limit; remaining tokens exposed to downstream policy.

**Semantic caching** compares "vector proximity of the prompt to prior requests"; requires Azure Managed Redis or a RediSearch-compatible external cache; implemented by the paired `llm-semantic-cache-store` and `llm-semantic-cache-lookup` policies over the Embeddings API.
**Scale units and regional gateways** scale the gateway. The docs explicitly warn this does not scale the AI backends, which must be deployed in the same regions.

**Security:** managed identities remove the need for API keys; OAuth via credential manager for apps and agents including MCP servers; `llm-content-safety` policy for prompt moderation via Azure AI Content Safety.
**Load balancing modes:** round-robin, weighted, priority-based, session-aware. Priority routing is recommended specifically to saturate PTU endpoints first.
**Circuit breaker** uses **dynamic trip duration from the backend's `Retry-After` header** rather than a fixed interval.
**`llm-emit-token-metric`** emits token metrics with custom dimensions for filtering in Azure Monitor; logging captures prompts, completions and token usage "for billing and auditing".
**Governance plane:** Azure API Center catalogue for APIs, MCP servers and skills; developer portals; policy toolkit; Copilot Studio connector.
**AI gateway in Microsoft Foundry is preview.**
**Hosted agent = container image or source zip → ACR → managed compute, dedicated Entra agent identity, dedicated endpoint.** Runs on Azure Container Apps in a **Micro VM** with its own subnet IP.
**Scaling is per session, not per replica.** No replica count, no warm pool. **Idle timeout 15 minutes; maximum session lifetime 30 days; permanent deletion after 30 days inactive.**
**Compute tiers 0.5/1, 1/2 and 2/4 vCPU-to-GiB; disk up to 20 GiB with ~20% reserved and invisible.**
**CPU and memory describe one session; billing is across all active sessions, so oversizing multiplies cost by concurrency.**
**Right-sizing is empirical:** run a representative workload, read Application Insights performance, compare peaks to allocation.
**Ceilings:** 100 active and 1,000 total revisions per agent; ~200 hosted agents per instance; ~250 projects per instance.

**AgentSchema:** AgentDefinition (`prompt` | `hosted` | `workflow`), AgentManifest (template + parameters + resources), ContainerAgent. **`{{ param }}` resolves at init; `${VAR}` resolves at deploy or run.**
**Two protocols: `responses`** (platform-managed conversation history) and **`invocations`** (no built-in conversation management).
**The schema has no skills field**, and tooling does not auto-download skills.
**`agent.yaml` and `agent.manifest.yaml` are documented as deprecated, superseded by a single `azure.yaml`** — while three other first-party surfaces still describe them as current.

**Nine deployment types** across standard/provisioned × global/data-zone/regional, plus batch variants and **Developer** (24-hour lifetime, no SLA, no residency guarantee). **Instant access (preview)** needs no deployment at all.
**Data at rest stays in the Azure geography for every type; inference processing location is what the type actually selects.**
**Provisioned is offered for low latency *variance*, not low latency.**
**Tool catalogue entries: remote MCP, local MCP, and custom (Logic Apps connectors converted to remote MCP).** Private tool catalogue scopes to one organisation.
**OpenAPI 3.0/3.1 tools with anonymous, API-key or managed-identity authentication.**
**Toolbox = curated tools behind one MCP-compatible endpoint**, with central credentials, versioning, governance and observability, and **tool implementations updatable without changing agent code.**

**The toolbox abstraction is not universal:** tool search, skills and reminder are toolbox-only; **function calling is direct-only because execution is client-side**; Bing grounding and computer use are direct-only.

**Three grounding layers:** the AI Search tool with inline citations; knowledge sources and knowledge bases for agentic retrieval; **Foundry IQ**, which automates chunking, embedding and permission enforcement and **decomposes queries into parallel subqueries and reranks.**
**Private VNet + AI Search tool requires Entra managed identity; key-based authentication is unsupported.**

**Session ≠ conversation.** Session is sandbox compute and filesystem; conversation is message history stored in Foundry and reachable from any channel. **Under Responses, reusing a session id does not replay prior messages.**

**Basic setup stores state in Microsoft-managed resources; standard setup stores threads, files and vector stores in your Storage, AI Search and Cosmos DB** — five containers, 1000 RU/s each, 3000 RU/s minimum, **different containers for the classic and new runtimes.**
**Threads persist until deleted; no default retention period is published; the documentation tells you to plan one.**
**Tracing is GA for prompt and hosted agents, preview for workflow and external agents.**
**Server-side tracing needs no code change** once Application Insights is connected. Client-side and local-OTLP paths layer on top; **any OTLP backend is supported.**
**Traces capture inputs, outputs, tool calls and results, retries, token consumption, latency and cost.** **Message content requires an explicit environment variable and is off by default.**

**Multi-agent semantic conventions** (with Cisco Outshift, on OTel + W3C Trace Context): `execute_task`; child spans `agent_to_agent_interaction`, `agent.state.management`, `agent_planning`, agent orchestration; attributes `tool_definitions`, `llm_spans`, `tool.call.arguments`, `tool.call.results`; an Evaluation event.
**The Conversation view exposes ordered actions, run steps and tool calls**, searchable by response or trace id — the reconstruct-without-re-running mechanism.
**External agents join the same surface by setting `gen_ai.agent.id` on every span.**
**Portal trace window is 90 days. Foundry states no retention period of its own: retention and sampling follow your Application Insights and Log Analytics configuration.**
**Querying telemetry needs Log Analytics Reader, plus Privileged Monitoring Data Reader on protected tables.**

**Published tracing practice: consistent span attribute names; correlate evaluation run ids with traces; redact before telemetry; treat traces as production data under the same controls and retention as logs.**
**Continuous evaluation samples responses at a set rate, surfaces metrics on a dashboard, and links evaluations to traces.** Sibling previews: **scheduled evaluations, red team scans, alerts.**
**Evaluation runs are skipped at an hourly ceiling — default 100 per hour.**
**Conversation-level evaluation lookback is capped at 7 days (168 hours).**
**Two sampling strategies: `random_sampling` (default) and `smart_filtering`, an undocumented service-managed heuristic biased toward "interesting" traces.**
**Evaluation levels `turn` and `conversation` cannot be mixed in one run.**
**Rubric evaluators score weighted 1–5 dimensions normalised to 0–1**, and are recommended as the *primary* quality measure, paired with built-ins for safety and groundedness.
**Human evaluation exists as a product feature — and no agreement between any built-in evaluator and human judgement is published.**

**SFT for most cases; DPO for preference and tone with exactly two completions per item and no reward model; RFT for objective domains with graders, no system messages, and a reference answer as the final message. Techniques stack.**
**Fine-tuning data floor is 10 examples; recommended start 50; hundreds to thousands for production; RFT ceiling 50,000; files JSONL, UTF-8 with BOM, under 512 MB.** **All of these are unsourced.**
**Workflow patterns: human-in-the-loop, sequential, group chat in the portal; sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat and magentic in the framework. A workflow can be exposed as an agent.**
**Handoff transfers ownership and full context; agent-as-tool retains ownership and controls what the sub-agent sees.**
**A connected agent may hold privileges the parent lacks. The delegation edge is a privilege boundary.**
**Publishing gives a stable endpoint and its own identity and RBAC scope — and project permissions do not transfer. Reassign after publishing.**

**Content filtering: four harm categories × four severity levels, default medium for text and low for images, prompt shields and protected-material detection on by default, filtering synchronous and separately billed.**
**Agent guardrails are preview, are block-only (no annotate-only mode), and fully override the model's guardrail. An omitted stage is an unscanned stage.**
**Guardrail inheritance: custom → underlying model deployment's → DefaultV2 only if the deployment has none.**

**Control plane versus data plane** is inherited from Azure, expressed as RBAC `actions` versus `dataActions`, and predicts most permission failures. **Owner and Contributor grant no data-plane access.**
**Foundry resource** (`Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts`, kind `AIServices`) is the governance boundary; **Foundry project** (`.../projects`) is a subresource and the development boundary.
**Connected resources — Storage, Key Vault, AI Search, Cosmos DB — have their own governance boundaries and are not governed by Foundry.** Their private endpoints are not auto-created.
**Some capabilities are resource-scoped only** (Translator is the given example); **fine-tune training cannot be project-isolated at all.**

**Foundry Control Plane** is reached by **Operate** and has five panes: Overview, Assets, Compliance, Quota, Admin. It requires **an AI gateway configured** for advanced governance, and is **portal-only — no API, CLI or template**.

**Five built-in roles:** Foundry Agent Consumer, Foundry User, Foundry Project Manager, Foundry Account Owner, Foundry Owner. **Renamed from Azure AI \* during the documentation's own lifetime; role IDs unchanged; use GUIDs in code.**
**Foundry Account Owner has no data actions. Foundry Owner is the only single role spanning both planes.** Fine-tuning needs both.
**Do not use roles beginning "Cognitive Services" or the "Azure AI Developer" role** for Foundry projects — the latter is scoped to Azure ML workspaces and Foundry hubs despite its name.
**Scopes include an individual agent**, but agent-scope assignments are evaluated only for endpoint access.
**Foundry User is auto-assigned on portal deployment and not on SDK or CLI deployment.**
**Entra ID scope is `https://ai.azure.com/.default` and requires a custom subdomain.** Agents, evaluations, datasets, Content Understanding and workflows **cannot** use API keys.

**Entra Agent ID:** an agent identity is a service principal created by a blueprint; **the agent identity, not the managed identity, needs the downstream RBAC**; a wrong token audience fails even with correct RBAC; blueprint principals cap at **250** agent identities and their creation permission **cannot be revoked**.
**Quota is per subscription, per region, per model, in TPM.** Usages API for consumption; Model Capacities API for availability. Fifteen minutes to propagate.

**Quota increases are ordered by receipt and prioritised by existing consumption; requests failing that test "might be denied".** Partner and community models cannot get increases at all. Agent Service file, message and tool limits cannot be increased.
**Capacity APIs return data for retired models.**
**Nine deployment types** across global, data-zone and regional processing scopes, plus **Developer** — no residency guarantee, twenty-four-hour lifetime, no SLA.
**Five lifecycle stages**; retirement returns `410 Gone`; "existing customer" for a Deprecated model is decided **per subscription**.

**Eighteen months from launch for GA models, set programmatically at launch; twelve for Anthropic, DeepSeek, Fireworks and Mistral.** Sixty days' notice for GA, thirty for preview. **Retirement dates are not extendable. Emergency retirement with unspecified shortened notice is reserved.**
**Three upgrade policies:** `OnceNewDefaultVersionAvailable`, `OnceCurrentVersionExpired`, `NoAutoUpgrade`. **Provisioned deployments are never auto-upgraded.**
**The Models API inverts the documentation's vocabulary:** `Deprecating` means still serving; `Deprecated` means retired.
**Service Health has no Foundry service** — alert on `Azure OpenAI Service`.

**Basic setup:** managed storage, no CMK, no BYO data, **no outbound isolation** — but inbound private endpoints work on any setup. **Standard** adds BYO Storage, AI Search and Cosmos DB plus CMK; **standard private** adds BYO VNet and no public egress.
**Subnet delegated to `Microsoft.App/environments`, `/27` or larger. Avoid `172.17.0.0/16`. No automatic cross-region failover.**

**Tracing is off by default** and only Foundry Account Owner or Foundry Owner can enable it. It captures prompts, completions, tool calls and metadata into Application Insights, readable by **Log Analytics Reader**. No default retention is stated.
**Logic Apps agent loops emit no traces or metrics.** Client-side tracing is preview. Traces take two to five minutes to appear.

**Continuous evaluation samples**, at a configurable rate, capped by `max_hourly_runs` defaulting to **100 per hour**; excess runs are skipped. Scheduled evaluations, red team scans and alerts are all preview.

**Guardrail policies are Azure Policy** scoped to subscription or resource group, with exceptions; need Owner or Resource Policy Contributor; take up to thirty minutes to appear and an unbounded scan to evaluate.

**Two built-in model-deployment policies** — approved-models (GA) and eligibility (preview, `onlyAllowDirectFromAzure` and `denyPreviewModels`). Evaluated at deployment time; **the model stays visible and Deploy is disabled with a reason.**
**Cost estimates exclude prompt agents, non-Foundry agents, PTU and discounts.** Cost Management and the invoice are authoritative.
**Project-level chargeback uses an automatic `project` tag, is preview, and excludes Azure Marketplace models.** Azure OpenAI appears under **Cognitive Services** in Cost Management.
**Fine-tuned models bill hourly for hosting even when unused. There is no hard spend cap.**

**Topology:** isolation is the default for production; colocation's price is "shared blast radius for production incidents, quota exhaustion, and misconfiguration". The business-group-resource-with-workload-projects pattern is explicitly not recommended.

**The fleet inventory covers Foundry agents, SRE Agent, Logic Apps agent loops and registered custom agents; not classic agents or OpenAI assistants; and is permission-relative, so two people see different estates.**

**Lifecycle operations differ by platform:** start/stop for hosted, published, SRE and Logic Apps; block/unblock for custom; **nothing but deletion for unpublished prompt agents**; and **stopping does not terminate in-flight runs**.
Agent behaviour is an authored artifact, separated into four kinds — **instructions, prompts, agents and skills** — with distinct trees and distinct application rules.
**Authoring source, packaging manifest and generated output are separated**, and the generated tree is declared non-canonical.
**RPI separates Research, Plan, Implement, Review and Follow-up** as gated phases with explicit return paths, rather than as a narrative order.
**Durable on-disk state under stable identifiers replaces session memory as the authority** for what was researched, planned, implemented and reviewed.
**Execution completion and acceptance outcome are distinct results**, and a completed phase is not an accepted one.
Review is decomposed into orientation, lens, severity normalisation and risk-scaled depth, so that two reviewers produce comparable findings.

**Untrusted content is data, not authority:** fetched pages, documents, repositories, tool output and issue bodies may not issue instructions, and embedded instructions are reported rather than obeyed.
**An agent may not record a human's approval.** Human review is a stop condition, not a checkbox the workflow can satisfy for itself.
**A gate may be advisory or authoritative, and the difference is a property of the tier it runs in** rather than of the check itself.
**Regex-graded behavioural checks test output shape, not correctness**, and the repository says so in its own documentation.
Missing dependencies are made to produce setup failures rather than silent passes.
Telemetry is opt-in, local, and redacted by default, with verbatim capture behind a separate explicit opt-in.
**The existence of a control is not evidence that the control works**, and this corpus is the clearest available worked example of the distinction at scale.
**A remote MCP server over streamable HTTP at `https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp`.** No authentication, no charge, no local model, no tenant. Use is subject to the Microsoft Learn Terms of Use.
**The endpoint is not browsable** and returns `405 Method Not Allowed` to a browser. It is for MCP clients.
**Three tools:** `microsoft_docs_search` (semantic search, `query`); `microsoft_docs_fetch` (page to markdown, `url`); `microsoft_code_sample_search` (`query`, optional `language`).
**The tool surface is explicitly dynamic.** Call `tools/list` on connection; never hardcode names, schemas or behaviour; treat 400 and 404 as a stale cache and refresh; listen for `listChanged`.
**"Not an Application Programming Interface (API) in the traditional sense."** Reach it through an agent framework, not by calling the endpoint directly.
**It fronts the Learn knowledge service** that also powers Ask Learn, Copilot for Azure, the Azure portal, Foundry and Copilot Studio — an advanced RAG system over chunked, embedded Learn content.

**Freshness is stated as cadence, not latency:** incremental refresh after content updates, full refresh once a day, content changing "usually on a daily basis". **No indexing-lag bound is published.**
**Scope is defined negatively:** "publicly available documentation, not training or user profile information". Locale, versioned-document and non-documentation coverage are unaddressed.
**No filtering parameter exists.** Narrowing is done by phrasing the question, and is therefore unauditable.
**Deprecated content redirects to "the next best appropriate content"**, so a fetch of a known URL can silently return something else.
**`maxTokenBudget` truncates search results only; fetch always returns the full page.** The default is not published.
**Rate limits exist and are not published**, along with no error code, no window and no retry guidance.
**General availability was declared 2025-11-07**, five months after first release, on the stated basis that usage "grew without issues".

**Configuration differs by host** — VS Code `.vscode/mcp.json` or user profile, Visual Studio built in, Foundry as a custom MCP tool with **Authentication: Unauthenticated**, Cline needing `"type": "streamableHttp"` — and there is also a plugin and a CLI.
**Declining trust does not fail loudly.** In VS Code "chat requests will continue without using the tools provided by the server."
**Trust is re-requested when a server's tools change**, so a dynamic tool list makes trust a recurring decision.
**The vendor documents that agents fail to call the tool** and recommends instructions as the remedy, without measuring either the problem or the fix.
**`applyTo` is a workspace-root-relative glob; without it an instructions file is not applied automatically.**
**Multiple instruction files are combined with no guaranteed order**, and matching may be semantic as well as glob-based.
**Receipt is checkable three ways:** the References section of a chat response, the chat customization Diagnostics view, and the Chat Debug view.
**`microsoft_docs_fetch` is the citation instrument**; `microsoft_docs_search` is the discovery instrument. Record the page, not the answer.
**Three build paths by service model:** Foundry (PaaS), Copilot Studio (SaaS), GPUs and containers (IaaS). Selection criteria: **technical capabilities, timeline, control requirements.**
**Foundry agent types:** **prompt agents** (declarative, no agent compute) and **hosted agents** (your containerized code on managed container compute).

**Foundry setup options:** **basic** for rapid prototyping, which **lacks network isolation**; **standard** with public networking for enterprise controls or private networking for confidential workloads.
**Declarative agents:** individual use, Copilot's orchestrator and models only, **no proactive interaction**, Microsoft 365 channels, hosted in Microsoft 365.
**Custom engine agents:** complex workflows, individual or group use, **full orchestration and model choice**, **proactive triggering**, internal and external channels, flexible hosting.

**Six published triggers for custom engine agents:** custom orchestration; own or domain-specific or multimodal models; group productivity; integrating an existing assistant; availability outside Microsoft 365; proactive messaging.
**Orchestrator ownership differs by tool:** Copilot Studio's own; Teams AI Action Planner; bring-your-own for Agents SDK and Foundry.
**Language support differs:** Teams AI (C#, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python); Agents SDK (C#, JavaScript, Python); Foundry (Python, C#); Copilot Studio (not applicable).
**Only Teams SDK, Microsoft 365 Agents SDK and Foundry agents can be published to the Microsoft Commercial Store** via the Agents Toolkit.
**Copilot Studio is "designed for small-scale deployments, such as department-level solutions."**

**Copilot Studio's stated limits:** less fine-grained control over API calls, actions and response formatting; less integrated pro-dev tooling than Agents Toolkit; **Adaptive Cards schema 1.6 and earlier**; slower feature availability.
**Tools connect via the Tool catalog, MCP and OpenAPI specifications**, with Logic Apps and Functions for serverless automation.
**The options are explicitly not mutually exclusive** — components on different platforms compose through MCP.

**Two Foundry-to-Microsoft-365 integration paths:** direct publish, which auto-provisions Azure Bot Service and Entra ID; or an Agents Toolkit proxy app for custom logic, SSO and multi-environment deployment.
**Microsoft IQ** groups **Work IQ**, **Fabric IQ**, **Foundry IQ** and **Web IQ**. Membership is stated as four on two pages and as three on three others. **Web IQ has no Learn documentation.**
**The durable carve-up is by provenance:** how people work; what the business is; what the organisation has written down; what the world says.
**Composition is by tool, not by planner.** "Each IQ workload is standalone, but you can use them together." No cross-layer ranking, arbitration or joint permission model is published.

**Work IQ protocols:** A2A at `https://workiq.svc.cloud.microsoft/a2a/` (v1.0 and v0.3 via `A2A-Version`; JSON-RPC; method in body; `contextId` for multi-turn; `Location` metadata for time-sensitive queries), remote MCP, REST, and local MCP via the `@microsoft/workiq` CLI.

**Work IQ auth: Entra delegated only. On-behalf-of supported. Application-only not supported.** In multitenant organisations the token issuer must be the user's home tenant or the call fails with `400 AuthenticationError`.
**Work IQ scope of data:** email, meetings and calendar, OneDrive and SharePoint documents, Teams messages, people and organisational context, Microsoft Planner plans, enterprise search results.
**Work IQ tool grammar:** "hundreds of operations into just 10 generic tools" — verbs plus resource paths, with runtime schema discovery so every source is "a self-describing interface".
**Work IQ Workspaces:** persistent SharePoint Embedded working storage inside the tenant boundary for long-running agent workflows.
**Work IQ policy:** broad permissions for boundaries, **a Rego policy engine** for per-request decisions on resource path, method, identity and data content; every tool invocation logged.

**Work IQ's Context layer is assembled from Copilot memory, the Microsoft 365 semantic index and Dataverse intelligence** — all pre-existing. The semantic index is "a superset of content within Microsoft Graph and ingested content from Copilot connectors."
**Work IQ CLI reached general availability on 16 June 2026**; preview builds 0.4.x and 0.5.x are unsupported and issues must be reproduced on a GA build.

**Foundry's Work IQ tool requires** a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence for the developer and every calling user; Foundry User and Foundry Project Manager roles; **Entra Global Administrator consent for `WorkIQAgent.Ask`**; and **does not support VNet integration**.
**Fabric IQ is a Fabric workload** containing ontology (preview), Power BI semantic model, Plan, Graph, Data agent and Operations agent, over OneLake.

**Ontology** = entity types, entity instances, properties, typed relationships with cardinality, **data bindings** to OneLake without copying, an **ontology graph** with lineage, and **NL2Ontology** routing to GQL or KQL.
**Ontologies can be generated from production Power BI semantic models** — bootstrap from trusted definitions rather than convene a committee.
**Ontology data is not live: upstream changes "need to be manually refreshed"** before appearing. Stated twice.
**Foundry IQ requires Azure AI Search.** Agentic retrieval is the engine; Foundry IQ is knowledge bases, sources, native Foundry integrations and a portal experience over it.

**Knowledge source types:** indexed (Blob, OneLake, SharePoint, existing indexes — with chunking, vectorisation, metadata and ACL synchronisation) and remote (SharePoint via Copilot Retrieval API, web via Grounding with Bing — nothing stored, always current).

**Retrieval reasoning effort:** minimal — 10 sources, no LLM, no planning, no synthesis; low — 3 sources, 3 subqueries, 5,000-token budget; medium — 5 sources, 5 subqueries, iterative search, 10,000-token budget. **Default `low`.** Planning models limited to gpt-4o, gpt-4.1 and gpt-5 series.

**Permission enforcement in Foundry IQ is opt-in and off by default:** "Unless support for out-of-the-box user permissions is explicitly stated in the knowledge source documentation, document-level access controls aren't automatically honored."
**Foundry IQ and Copilot knowledge sources are explicitly not interoperable** in either direction.

**Web Knowledge Source waives protections:** the Data Protection Addendum does not apply, data flows outside the Azure compliance and geographic boundary, and use "waives all elevated Government Community Cloud security and compliance commitments to include data sovereignty".

**Agentic retrieval bills by token across two services** — Azure AI Search for retrieval and reranking, Azure OpenAI for planning and synthesis — against the classic pipeline's per-query semantic-ranker charge.

**The 36% figure compares medium against minimal reasoning effort of the same product**, averaged over five datasets (59 → 80, +21 absolute, range 16% to 60%). The Learn FAQ restates it as against "traditional single-shot RAG". **The blog did not measure that.**
**Source naming matters measurably:** blurred or cross-domain descriptions cost up to 43 points of source-selection recall; a good name survives an adversarial description.
**Purview's four capability groups:** insights and analytics; ready-to-use prompt data-loss policies; data risk assessments for oversharing; compliance controls.
**The oversharing argument:** generative AI "amplifies the problem of oversharing data" by surfacing content that is "obsolete, over-permissioned, or lacking governance controls."
**Default data risk assessment runs weekly over the top 100 SharePoint sites**, and, once configured, the **top 100 Fabric workspaces**.
**Assessment detail is organised as Identify, Protect, Monitor.**

**Remediation options:** restrict access by label via DLP; SharePoint Restricted Content Discovery to exempt sites; auto-labelling for unlabelled sensitive files; retention policies deleting content unaccessed for three years.
**Item-level actions:** Resolve, Apply sensitivity label, Notify owner, Remove sharing link — the last flagged as disruptive and to be used sparingly.

**Stated limits:** 200,000 items per location; counts possibly inaccurate above 100,000 files per location; OneDrive unsupported for item-level scanning; maximum 10 SharePoint sites for item-level scanning.
**Stated latencies:** 24 hours for policy data; 48 hours for custom assessment results; 4-day delay on first default assessment; 30-day expiry on custom results.
**Without an explicit policy, Copilot in Fabric and Security Copilot audit the event but not the prompts and responses.**

**Activity explorer captures** activity type and user, timestamp, AI app category and app, app accessed in, sensitive information types, files referenced and sensitive files referenced; prompts and responses are permission-gated.
**Workload taxonomy:** Copilot experiences and agents; Enterprise AI apps; Other AI apps.
**Defender's AI BOM** covers "application components, data, and AI artifacts from code to cloud."
**Automatic continuous discovery across five services:** Azure OpenAI Service, Azure AI Foundry, Azure Machine Learning, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI.
**Dependency scanning** names TensorFlow, PyTorch and Langchain; covers IaC misconfigurations and container image vulnerabilities.
**Four IaC AI security checks:** private endpoints; restricted endpoints; managed identity; identity-based authentication.
**Attack path analysis** targets "toxic combinations", with grounding and fine-tuning named as the data-exposure moments.
**Named AI-native attacks:** prompt injection, wallet attacks, model theft, data poisoning, plus data breach and denial of service.
**From 1 July 2026, agent-level discovery and posture require a Microsoft Agent 365 licence.**
